section: 4.1 Growth rates per well (spline based estimate)
text:
4.1 Growth rates per well (spline based estimate)
Using the tool growthrates to estimate mu_max. I have found this works a lot better than gcplyr and is more convenient than using another tool outside of R. Nonparametric estimate growth rates by spline is very fast. Fitting to a model takes more time resources. Generally it is best to try multiple approaches and to visualize/check the data to make sure it makes sense.
Unlike upstream, the streptomycin-dosed wells are kept here.


Show/hide code
gcurves_thin_sm <- df |>
  # exclude blanks, but keep every streptomycin concentration
  filter(strainID != "blank") |>
  # need to add a small floor for numerical stability for the spline fit
  mutate(
    OD600_rollmean_spline = if_else(OD600_rollmean == 0, 1e-3, OD600_rollmean)
  ) |>
  # make uniq id
  mutate(id = paste0(plate_name, "|", well))


Smoothing splines are a quick method to estimate maximum growth. The method is called nonparametric, because the growth rate is directly estimated from the smoothed data without being restricted to a specific model formula. From growthrates documentation:

The method was inspired by an algorithm of Kahm et al. (2010), with different settings and assumptions. In the moment, spline fitting is always done with log-transformed data, assuming exponential growth at the time point of the maximum of the first derivative of the spline fit. All the hard work is done by function smooth.spline from package stats, that is highly user configurable. Normally, smoothness is automatically determined via cross-validation. This works well in many cases, whereas manual adjustment is required otherwise, e.g. by setting spar to a fixed value [0, 1] that also disables cross-validation.



Show/hide code
set.seed(45278)
many_spline <- growthrates::all_splines(
  OD600_rollmean_spline ~ hours | id,
  data = gcurves_thin_sm,
  spar = 0.5
)

readr::write_rds(
  many_spline,
  here::here(data_interim, "one_carbon_spline_fits.rds")
)

# get results
gr_per_well <- growthrates::results(many_spline) |>
  tidyr::separate('id', into = c("plate_name", "well")) |>
  left_join(distinct(dplyr::select(
    df,
    -seconds,
    -hours,
    -OD600,
    -OD600_rollmean

title: 05.A Carbon source platemap
text:
Converts the Carbon_platemap*.xlsx well maps in data/raw/20260601_single_carbon_growth into a single tidy platemap that the next notebook joins onto the LogPhase 600 reads.
This code is ported from scripts/10_one_carbon_gcurves_logphase/01_carbon_source_platemap_format.R in hambiEvoEnvCoexist. The parsing is unchanged: the plates were run jointly, so the platemap describes all four species that were on them (HAMBI_0403, HAMBI_1287, HAMBI_1896, HAMBI_1977). Restricting to the two species this project cares about happens in the next notebook, so that the plate QC views still show every well as it was actually run.


The spreadsheets are irregular: each sheet holds several plate blocks stacked vertically, and a block is only identifiable by scanning for its “Plate N” header. Within a block we read

the well-column header row (1..12),
the row-letter rows (A..H, read until column B goes empty),
the “Medium/carbon source” row, and
the “Streptomycin (ug/ml)” row.

The carbon source is resolved through the sheet’s merged-cell ranges rather than forward-filled across the row. This matters: some blocks (uninoculated “Control” wells) deliberately have no medium entry and must not inherit the value from a neighbouring block.




“control” -> “Control” (inconsistent capitalisation in the sources).
Strip the “M9MM with” prefix and ” + Str” suffix from carbon_source; the streptomycin column already carries the “+Str” distinction.
Attach the raw LogPhase filename for each plate via plate_file_maps.




Three corrections cannot be derived from the spreadsheets and are applied explicitly in the “Per-file corrections” section below:

Carbon_platemap_2: source typo, “shicimic acid” -> “shikimic acid”.
Carbon_platemap_4: the Streptomycin row is all zeros, including in the “+Str” well-columns, so columns 9-10 and 11-12 are set to 10 and 512.
Carbon_platemap_5: the well-column labels for the two right-hand blocks are transposed in the source sheet – see swap_column_blocks().

In every other platemap checked, the Streptomycin row is internally consistent (0 outside “+Str”/“Control” blocks, 10 for the ANC/EVO 1977 columns and 512 for the ANC/EVO 1287 columns inside a “+Str” block), so the spreadsheet values are trusted as-is.






ImportantCorrection 3 carries more weight here than upstream



In hambiEvoEnvCoexist only the streptomycin-free columns 1-4 were analysed, so the Carbon_platemap_5 block transposition never touched a well that made it into a figure. This project analyses the +Str wells, which are exactly the columns that correction swaps. The evidence for the swap is in the reads themselves — columns 9-12 are empty across all 8 rows (never inoculated, i.e. the Control block) while columns 5-8 grew, and their per-column growth mirrors the strep-0 block in columns 1-4 strain for strain. Worth re-checking against the bench notebook before these results go into a manuscript.


Carbon_platemap_7.8 and Carbon_platemap_7.8_2 differ structurally: each plate has no Streptomycin row at all (this batch doesn’t test streptomycin dosing), and the uninoculated block’s well cells are left empty rather than labelled “Control”. Both are handled generically rather than as per-file corrections: a missing Streptomycin row parses as blank and later defaults to “0”, and an empty well is flagged “blank” the same way a strain == "Control" well is.

2.6 Per-file correction helpers


Show/hide code
# Exchange two blocks of well-columns within a plate. Used where the source
# sheet's well-column header labels are transposed relative to the physical
# plate: the labels parsed under `from` actually describe the wells in `to` and
# vice versa, so the records are relabelled symmetrically.
#
# `well` is rebuilt from `row` and the corrected column so that it stays
# consistent with `column`.
swap_column_blocks <- function(records, from, to, plates = NULL) {
  stopifnot(length(from) == length(to))

  in_scope <- if (is.null(plates)) TRUE else records$plate %in% plates

  records |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      column = dplyr::case_when(
        !in_scope ~ column,
        column %in% from ~ to[match(column, from)],
        column %in% to ~ from[match(column, to)],
        .default = column
      ),
      well = stringr::str_c(row, column)
    )
}

text:
2.8 Per-file corrections


Show/hide code
# Not reproducible from the spreadsheets themselves (see header note).

# (1) Carbon_platemap_2: source spreadsheet typo
source_records$platemap_2 <- source_records$platemap_2 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    carbon_source = stringr::str_replace(
      carbon_source,
      "^shicimic acid$",
      "shikimic acid"
    )
  )

# (2) Carbon_platemap_4: Streptomycin row is all zeros, including in the "+Str"
# well-columns (9-10 = ANC/EVO 1977, 11-12 = ANC/EVO 1287)
source_records$platemap_4 <- source_records$platemap_4 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    streptomycin_ug_ml = dplyr::case_when(
      column %in% c(9, 10) ~ "10.0",
      column %in% c(11, 12) ~ "512.0",
      .default = streptomycin_ug_ml
    )
  )

# (3) Carbon_platemap_5: the well-column labels of the "+Str" block and the
# uninoculated "Control" block are transposed in the source sheet. As parsed,
# columns 5-8 come out as Control and columns 9-12 as the "+Str" strain wells.
# The reads show the opposite, unambiguously:
#
#   * columns 9-12 are empty across all 8 rows -- never inoculated, i.e. the
#     Control block;
#   * columns 5-8 grew, and their per-column growth mirrors the strep-0 block
#     in columns 1-4 strain for strain (1977 ANC/EVO, then 1287 ANC/EVO), which
#     is exactly the "+Str" block layout.
#
# So the two blocks are exchanged: 5<->9, 6<->10, 7<->11, 8<->12. Columns 1-4
# (the streptomycin-free wells this project actually analyses) are untouched.
source_records$platemap_5 <- source_records$platemap_5 |>
  swap_column_blocks(from = 5:8, to = 9:12)

attach_plate_file <- function(records, plate_file_map) {
  records |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      plate_file = plate_file_map[stringr::str_extract(plate, "[0-9]+")]
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(
      plate,
      well,
      row,
      column,
      evo_hist,
      strainID,
      streptomycin_ug_ml,
      carbon_source,
      plate_file

    \(records, nm) attach_plate_file(records, plate_file_maps[[nm]])

  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # well format must match the samplesheet, e.g. "A01" not "A1"
    well = stringr::str_c(
      stringr::str_extract(well, "^[A-H]"),
      stringr::str_pad(
        stringr::str_extract(well, "\\d+"),
        width = 2,
        pad = "0",
        side = "left"
      )
    ),
    strainID = dplyr::if_else(
      strainID != "",
      stringr::str_c(
        "H",
        stringr::str_pad(strainID, width = 4, pad = "0", side = "left")
      ),
      strainID
    ),
    streptomycin_ug_ml = stringr::str_remove(streptomycin_ug_ml, "\\.0")

  # uninoculated wells are flagged "blank" across every descriptive column.
  # Most sheets label these wells "Control" in the strain cell;
  # Carbon_platemap_7.8 and _2 instead leave the strain cell empty, hence the
  # is.na() check.
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      c(evo_hist, strainID, streptomycin_ug_ml, carbon_source),
      \(x) {
        dplyr::if_else(
          is.na(evo_hist) | evo_hist == "Control" | carbon_source == "Control",
          "blank",
          x
        )
      }
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    streptomycin_ug_ml = dplyr::if_else(
      streptomycin_ug_ml == "",
      "0",
      streptomycin_ug_ml
    ),
    # fixing inconsistent carbon source names across sheets
    carbon_source = dplyr::case_when(
      carbon_source == "valine" ~ "L-valine",
      carbon_source == "malic acid (malate)" ~ "malate",
      carbon_source == "4-hydrobenzoic acid" ~ "4-Hydroxybenzoic acid",
      carbon_source == "cysteine" ~ "L-cysteine",
      carbon_source == "arginine" ~ "L-arginine",
      .default = carbon_source
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(carbon_source_classes, by = dplyr::join_by(carbon_source))

title: 04.B Formatting serial transfer growth curves
text:
Strain naming convention: 1287 = Citrobacter koseri 1287, 1977 = Pseudomonas chlororaphis 1977, A = Ancestral/Streptomycin sensitive, E = Evolved/Streptomycin resistant.
Growth media convention: M9MM = M9 minimal media with glucose as the sole carbon source and supplemented with casamino acids. R2A = Reasoner’s 2 broth (complex growth medium).
This experiment ran for five 48-hour growth cycles (240 hours of growth total) where each well was serially diluted to a concentration of 10-4 (10,000 fold dilution) and then placed back in the incubating plate reader.
In this notebook we read the five cycle exports, join them to the samplesheet, and smooth them. Each cycle export holds the 1977 plate on sheet 2 and the 1287 plate on sheet 5.

2.3 Functions
This function collects all the data from monocultures and cocultures for the selected species pair. Only monoculture data from streptomycin concentrations tested in co-cultures is included.


Show/hide code
collect_sp_pairs <- function(df, competition_pair, strep_thresh) {
  strainpairs <- stringr::str_split(competition_pair, "_")[[1]]
  df %>%
    mutate(streptomycin = if_else(plate_name == "plate01", 0, streptomycin)) %>%
    mutate(strainID = make_strainID(evolution, strain)) %>%
    filter(strainID %in% strainpairs) %>%
    filter(str_detect(culture_type, "diffusion", negate = T)) %>%
    filter(streptomycin <= {{ strep_thresh }}) %>%
    filter(
      (culture_type == "coculture" &
        competition_pair == {{ competition_pair }}) |
        culture_type == "monoculture"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      culture_type = factor(
        culture_type,
        levels = c("monoculture", "coculture")
      )
    )
}


This function plots the output from the collect_sp_pairs function.


Show/hide code
plot_sp_pairs <- function(df, title) {
  df_cl <- df %>%
    mutate(seconds = seconds - seconds %% 1200) %>%
    mutate(hours = seconds / 3600) %>%
    summarize(
      y = mean(OD600_rollmean),
      sd = sd(OD600_rollmean),
      n = n(),
      .by = c(hours, strainID, streptomycin, competition_pair, culture_type)
    ) %>%
    mutate(ymin = y - 1.96 * sd / sqrt(n), ymax = y + 1.96 * sd / sqrt(n))

  ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = df_cl,
      aes(
        x = hours,
        y = y,
        color = strainID
      ),
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
      data = df_cl,
      aes(
        x = hours,
        ymin = ymin,
        ymax = ymax,
        fill = strainID,
        group = interaction(strainID, streptomycin, culture_type)
      ),
      alpha = 0.5
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = df,
      aes(
        x = hours,
        y = OD600_rollmean,
        color = strainID,
        group = interaction(well, plate_name)
      ),
      alpha = 0.25,
      linewidth = 0.25
    ) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Hours", y = "OD600") +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = seq(0, 48, 12),
      labels = seq(0, 48, 12)
    ) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      y = "Optical density (600 nm), log scale",
      x = "Hours",
      title = {{ title }}
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = straincols) +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = straincols) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(trans = "log", breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1)) +
    ggplot2::facet_grid(culture_type ~ streptomycin) +
    ggplot2::theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}

title: 03.A Formatting co-culture growth curves from Logphase 600
text:
The ancestral (streptomycin sensitive) and evolved (streptomycin resistant) forms of HAMBI_1287 and HAMBI_1977 were grown on adjacent 0.22 μm membrane-separated wells in a Verasys co-culture plate. The membrane allows free diffusion of resources and metabolic byproducts but not cells. Note that due to the unique format of the plate rows A and H do not contain any data. The plates differ by streptomycin concentration as indicated below. Measurements were collected with a Biotek Logphase 600 microplate reader.
In this notebook we read the plate reader exports, join them to the samplesheets, smooth them, and inspect every well.

title: 02.B Growth statistics on Biolog Ecoplates
text:
Here we estimate maximum specific growth rate (\(\mathrm{\mu_{max}}\)) and total metabolic output (area under the growth curve) for every well of the Biolog Ecoplates formatted in the prior step.
We use growthrates to estimate \(\mathrm{\mu_{max}}\). I have found this works a lot better than gcplyr and is more convenient than using another tool outside of R. Nonparametric estimation of growth rates by spline is very fast. Fitting to a model takes more time resources. Generally it is best to try multiple approaches and to visualize/check the data to make sure it makes sense (Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution).

title: 02.A Formatting growth curves from Synergy H1
text:
The ancestral (streptomycin sensitive) and evolved (streptomycin resistant) forms of HAMBI_1287 and HAMBI_1977 were grown on Biolog Ecoplates. These are basically a set of 32 different carbon compounds in 3 replicated sets on a 96 well plate. Microbial species or communities grown on these carbon compounds respire and reduce some dye to a purple color which is then measured on a Synergy H1 multimode microplate reader.
In this notebook we read the output from the Synergy H1 plate reader, join it to the samplesheets, smooth it, and inspect every well.

text:
4.2 Join with metadata to remove unused samples
Grouping by plate and well, we calculate a five point centered rolling mean. This reduces the jaggedness of the curves and also makes the resulting saved data file smaller.


Show/hide code
ecoplate_gcurves_sm <- bind_rows(plate01, plate02, plate03) %>%
  left_join(
    bind_rows(samplesheet01, samplesheet02, samplesheet03),
    by = join_by(well, plate_name)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(plate_name, well) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    OD600_rollmean = slider::slide_dbl(OD600, mean, .before = 2, .after = 2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  relocate(OD600_rollmean, .after = "OD600")

# save output for later use
readr::write_tsv(
  ecoplate_gcurves_sm,
  here::here(data_processed, "gcurves_smooth.tsv")
)

title: 02.C Strain growth on Biolog Ecoplates
text:
The Biolog Ecoplates utilize tetrazolium reduction to measure the metabolic response of bacterial cells to different carbon substrates. Oxidized tetrazolium salt is water soluble, colorless in solution, and can freely diffuse into bacterial cells. Once inside the cell, tetrazolium is reduced by reducing agents like NADH an NADPH which are generated via cellular metabolism and catabolism. Once reduced tetrazolium is transformed into pink product. This assay measures the accumulation of reduced tetrazolium (colormetric absorbance at 590 nm) and hence the accumulation and concentration of reducing agents from cellular metabolism. This process will reflect both the concentration of cells in solution and per-capita concentration of reductant from central metabolism. There is a useful overview of the Tetrazolium colorometric procedure available here.
In the prior step we imported, smoothed, and calculated summary statistics for the species growth on Biolog Ecoplates. Here we will do some simple plots and analysis of the growth data on different carbon sources from the ecoplates.

title: 03.B Growth statistics for co-culture plates
text:
Here we estimate maximum specific growth rate (\(\mathrm{\mu_{max}}\)) and total growth (area under the growth curve) for every well of the co-culture plates formatted in the prior step.
We use growthrates to estimate \(\mathrm{\mu_{max}}\). I have found this works a lot better than gcplyr and is more convenient than using another tool outside of R. Nonparametric estimation of growth rates by spline is very fast. Fitting to a model takes more time resources. Generally it is best to try multiple approaches and to visualize/check the data to make sure it makes sense (Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution).

title: 04.A Serial transfer pilot
text:
Strain naming convention: 1287 = Citrobacter koseri 1287, 1977 = Pseudomonas chlororaphis 1977, A = Ancestral/Streptomycin sensitive, E = Evolved/Streptomycin resistant.
This is the pilot that preceded the main serial transfer experiment. Its purpose was to pick a serial dilution factor: each transfer was carried out at three different dilutions in parallel so we could see which one gives a full growth cycle inside a 48 hour window.

d1 = 100,000 fold dilution
d2 = 1,000 fold dilution
d3 = 50 fold dilution

Plates are named h<hours>_d<dilution>, so h96_d2 is the 1,000 fold dilution read at the 96 hour timepoint.

title: 04.C Serial transfer of co-culture pairs
text:
Strain naming convention: 1287 = Citrobacter koseri 1287, 1977 = Pseudomonas chlororaphis 1977, A = Ancestral/Streptomycin sensitive, E = Evolved/Streptomycin resistant.
Growth media convention: M9MM = M9 minimal media with glucose as the sole carbon source and supplemented with casamino acids. R2A = Reasoner’s 2 broth (complex growth medium).
This experiment ran for five 48-hour growth cycles (240 hours of growth total) where each well was serially diluted to a concentration of 10-4 (10,000 fold dilution) and then placed back in the incubating plate reader.
Here we inspect every cycle, drop the well pairs that grew where nothing should have grown, and plot the competition time course with all five cycles joined end to end.

title: 05.B Growth curves on M9MM + single carbon
text:
Each strain was grown in M9 minimal medium with a single compound supplied as the sole carbon source, at three streptomycin concentrations, and read on a Biotek Logphase 600. This notebook joins the LogPhase reads to the platemap from the previous step, smooths them, and inspects every plate.
The plates were run jointly with hambiEvoEnvCoexist and carry four species. The QC views below show every well as it was run; the saved table is restricted to the two species this project uses (HAMBI_1287 and HAMBI_1977) plus the uninoculated blanks.
Streptomycin dosing is per species — HAMBI_1977 wells were dosed at 10 μg/ml and HAMBI_1287 wells at 512 μg/ml, alongside the streptomycin-free wells. So each species has two levels, not a shared gradient.
